title: Forward hum
purpose: Find an easy, buzzy hum with your tongue forward and a small smile, then open it into vowels and m-words, listening for a brighter sound.
instructions: Breathe in easily and hum on a comfortable note, lips gently closed and teeth apart.
Rest your tongue forward, behind your bottom teeth, and add a small smile. Listen for the hum getting brighter. A tingle on your lips is a sign of easy voicing, not the goal.
Open the hum into vowels without a break: mmmee, mmmaa, mmmoo.
Then words that start with m, lingering on the m at first: meet, many, maybe, Mary, magic.

primary_cue.text: Hum with your tongue forward and a small smile.

cues.text: Hum with your tongue forward and a small smile.
Add a small smile and hum again.
Start with a soft breath out through your nose, then let the hum begin: hhhmmm.
Picture the sound landing just in front of your lips.
Start the hum very quietly, then let it grow a little, listening for brightness.

practice_task.prompt_text: Hum with your tongue forward, then say: mmmee, mmmaa, mmmoo — meet, many, maybe, Mary, magic.

check_questions.text: Listen back. Did the hum and the words sound brighter, and feel easy?

options.label: Easy, but I can't hear a change yet
It took effort or felt tight

check_questions.text: Where did you notice the buzz most? (Only a clue about easy voicing; every answer is fine.)

dose_guidance.text: No set number. A few unhurried rounds, then move on while it still feels easy. Short and often beats long and rare.

expected_observations: A light buzz around your lips and face, which tends to come with easy voicing.
Over days, a brighter sound carrying into the words after the hum.
common_misunderstandings: The buzz isn't resonance. Where you feel it says more about easy voicing and pitch, so listen for brightness instead.
Pitch alone doesn't decide how a voice sounds.
Lighter doesn't mean quieter or whispery.
stop_conditions: Anything hurts, feels tight or scratchy, or your voice turns hoarse: that usually means too much, too soon.
Rest your voice and come back another day, starting smaller.
If hoarseness or discomfort lasts or keeps coming back, see a GP, or a speech and language therapist who works with voices.
adaptations: Stay with the hum and the vowels for as long as you like.
limitations: Written for Lilt for practising on your own. Lilt can't check your technique, and it doesn't replace a speech and language therapist.
Lilt can't feel where your voice buzzes, and its resonance comparison is rough and only works on held vowels, so your ears and what you report lead here.
